title: Real-Time at Scale
description: Learn how to design a real-time chat system with WebSockets, message ordering, presence tracking, group messaging, and end-to-end encryption.

segments.text: Two billion people use WhatsApp daily. Every message delivered in milliseconds, in order, with end-to-end encryption. Let's design a system that can do that.

HTTP is request-response. The client asks, the server answers. But chat needs the server to push messages instantly. Polling every second? That's millions of wasted requests. We need a persistent connection.

WebSockets solve this. A single TCP connection stays open between client and server. Either side can send data at any time. One connection per user, always listening, always ready to deliver messages instantly.

With millions of concurrent connections, you need a connection manager. It tracks which user is connected to which server. When Alice sends a message to Bob, the system looks up Bob's server and routes the message there.

But what if Bob is offline? The message gets stored in a persistent queue. When Bob reconnects, the system delivers all queued messages in order. This is the store-and-forward pattern — essential for reliability.
Here's a tricky scenario. Alice sends two messages fast: 'I got the job!' then 'Just kidding.' They arrive at the server on different paths.
segments.thought_prompt: How do you guarantee Bob sees these messages in the correct order?

segments.text: Message ordering uses sequence numbers per conversation. Each message gets a monotonically increasing ID. The client renders messages sorted by this sequence, regardless of network arrival order. Server-assigned timestamps prevent clock skew issues.

The presence system tracks who's online. Each heartbeat from a client resets a timer. If the timer expires, the user is marked offline. But broadcasting presence updates to everyone would be expensive — so we update lazily, only when someone opens a chat.

Group messaging multiplies complexity. A message to a group of five hundred members must be delivered to all of them. We fan-out through a message queue — each member's delivery is independent. Failed deliveries get retried without blocking others.
WhatsApp claims it can't read your messages, even though its servers relay them. How is that possible if the server is in the middle of every conversation?
segments.thought_prompt: How can end-to-end encryption work when the server routes every message?

segments.text: End-to-end encryption means the client encrypts before sending, and only the recipient's client can decrypt. The server sees only ciphertext. The Signal Protocol uses a key exchange so both sides derive shared secrets without the server ever knowing them.

A chat system at scale needs WebSockets for real-time delivery, store-and-forward for offline users, sequence numbers for ordering, heartbeats for presence, fan-out for groups, and E2E encryption for privacy. Simple on the surface, deeply complex underneath.
